The Crucible. Arthur Miller's 1953 play dramatizes the 1692 Salem witch trials, depicting a community consumed by fear, accusation, and moral compromise. The protagonist John Proctor, a farmer drawn into the hysteria, becomes a test case for integrity and the consequences of bearing witness to injustice.

The play was written as an allegory for McCarthyism and the anti-communist witch hunts of nineteen-fifties America. Its critique of mass hysteria and coerced confession parallels contemporary political persecution. John Proctor is accused alongside many townspeople. Initially he considers confessing to save his life but ultimately refuses to sign a false confession, choosing execution over moral surrender.

The play's title refers both to the literal crucible, a melting pot, and to John Proctor's crucifixion—a spiritual reckoning where integrity requires sacrifice. Abigail Williams is a servant girl whose accusation begins the trials. She is depicted as manipulative and driven by desire for John Proctor, suggesting personal vengeance beneath the religious fervor. The play's final act takes place in the courthouse and shows how the machinery of law and authority becomes a tool for injustice when driven by panic and self-interest.

Miller's historical research grounded the play in actual trial records. It became one of the most frequently taught works in American high schools. Arthur Miller created this political response to McCarthyism and defense of conscience. The Salem witch trials are the historical event, and Miller's dramatization raises questions about collective madness and institutional evil.

Death of a Salesman is Miller's other major work, exploring individual moral reckoning against social pressure. The Scarlet Letter is another American work set in Puritan New England, exploring sin, shame, and public judgment. A Raisin in the Sun is a contemporary play examining how individuals maintain dignity and family integrity under systemic oppression. The Crucible remains a powerful examination of how fear corrupts justice.
